summary: Updates RFC 6775 and RFC 8505 to enable proxy services for IPv6 Neighbor Discovery by Routing Registrars called Backbone Routers. They sit along the wireless edge of a backbone and join several wireless links into one multi-link subnet. It is standards-track.

eli5.summary: Many small wireless networks can be made to act like one big network. Special routers at the edge speak up on behalf of the little devices so everyone can find each other.

subtitle: Backbone Routers that answer IPv6 Neighbor Discovery on behalf of wireless nodes, so many wireless links can act as one subnet.

tldr.problem: IPv6 Neighbor Discovery relies on multicast, which is typically broadcast over wireless links. That wastes bandwidth and battery, and duplicate address detection often fails on wireless.
tldr.mechanism: Nodes register their addresses with a 6LoWPAN Backbone Router (6BBR), which keeps a Binding Table and does the Neighbor Discovery on the backbone for them, either as a Routing Proxy or as a Bridging Proxy.
tldr.outcome: Several wireless links plus a backbone can be federated into one Multi-Link Subnet without flooding the wireless side. The scheme still needs the backbone and every router to be trusted.

today: RFC 8929 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2020. It updates RFC 6775 and RFC 8505, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated itself.

sections.title: Why Wireless Needs a Proxy
sections.content:
Ethernet bridging gives wired networks an efficient broadcast service, and IPv6 Neighbor Discovery (ND) was designed around it. On Low-Power and Lossy Networks (LLNs) and local wireless networks, multicast is typically broadcast on the radio, so a Neighbor Solicitation sent to a Solicited-Node Multicast Address reaches most wireless nodes anyway. That can consume enough bandwidth to hurt unicast service, and it forces sleepy battery-powered nodes to keep their radios on.

Duplicate Address Detection (DAD) also often fails to find duplicates over wireless. The RFC notes that IPv6 addresses rarely conflict mostly because of the entropy of 64-bit Interface IDs, not because DAD works well.

One fix is a Multi-Link Subnet (MLSN), in which each link, including the backbone, is its own broadcast domain but they share one subnet. This RFC defines ND proxies, called 6BBRs, at the edge between the LLNs and the backbone. It updates RFC 6775 and RFC 8505.
sections.eli5: Shouting across the whole wireless playground makes everyone listen and wastes their battery. The fix is to let a helper answer for the quiet kids instead.

sections.title: Registration and the 6BBR
sections.content:
Instead of guessing which addresses to proxy by snooping, which the RFC says has been found unreliable, the address is signaled explicitly. A 6LoWPAN Node (6LN) registers its IPv6 addresses with a Neural 6LoWPAN Router (6LR) by sending a Neighbor Solicitation carrying an Extended Address Registration Option (EARO), as in RFC 8505. If the 6LR is a 6BBR, the 6LN is both the Registered Node and the Registering Node. Otherwise a 6LoWPAN Border Router (6LBR) proxies the registration to the 6BBR on the node's behalf.

The 6BBR then performs ND on its backbone interface for the Registered Addresses, with no broadcast over the wireless medium. The topologies covered are an access link (for example Wi-Fi, where the 6BBR can sit in the access point) and a route-over mesh, where the 6LBR is the mesh root and registers addresses to the 6BBR.

An address may be registered to more than one 6BBR for availability. The primary 6BBR is the one with the highest 64-bit EUI-64 address among those sharing the same registration. If a Registering Node loses a 6BBR it MUST increment the Transaction ID (TID) when it re-registers, which forces the state to move to the new 6BBR.
sections.eli5: Each device tells its nearest helper 'this is my name'. The helper writes it down and answers for the device whenever anyone on the backbone asks.

sections.title: The Binding Table and Its Three States
sections.content:
Each 6BBR keeps a Binding Table. A Binding holds the Registered Address, information on the Registering Node, the EARO with its Registration Ownership Verifier (ROVR) and TID, and a state. The state is Tentative, Reachable or Stale.

  • Tentative: DAD is running over the backbone for TENTATIVE_DURATION. A conflicting NA or NS(DAD) with a different ROVR removes the Binding and the Registering Node is told Duplicate Address (status 1). When the timer elapses the Binding becomes Reachable and the Registering Node gets status 0 (Success).
  • Reachable: an active registration. Lookup and NUD messages SHOULD be answered with the Override flag not set. A fresher registration for the same ROVR removes the Binding and returns status 4 (Removed). An older one is answered with status 3 (Moved). When the Registration Lifetime ends, the Binding becomes Stale.
  • Stale: the 6BBR does not defend the address, but tracks backbone peers that still point to it. Before answering a lookup it MUST first run a NUD to the Registering Node. When STALE_DURATION elapses, the Binding MUST be removed.

The ROVR tells duplication (different ROVR) from movement (same ROVR, different TID), and the TID orders registrations so the freshest wins.
sections.eli5: The helper's list has three kinds of entries: 'just arrived, checking nobody else has this name', 'here and active', and 'maybe gone, check before answering'.

sections.title: Routing Proxy and Bridging Proxy
sections.content:
A 6BBR works in one of two modes. A Routing Proxy acts as an IPv6 border router with full link-layer isolation and proxies Global and Unique Local Addresses, but not link-local ones. It MUST put its own Layer 2 address in the SLLAO of the RS messages and the TLLAO of the NA messages it generates, and it installs a host route to the Registered Address. This mode is required when the LLN uses a different link-layer address format than the backbone, such as EUI-64 versus EUI-48.

A Bridging Proxy preserves forwarding continuity at the link layer and appears as an IPv6 host on the backbone. It MUST use the Registering Node's Layer 2 address in the SLLAO and TLLAO, proxies ND for all unicast addresses including link-local, and preferably forwards lookups to the node as unicast so the node can answer itself.

When a node moves to another 6BBR, the old 6BBR SHOULD send gratuitous NAs (and redirects) to peers that cached its link-layer address. If a peer misses it, the stale entry is eventually fixed by NUD.
sections.eli5: One kind of helper speaks in its own name and passes messages along. The other kind speaks with the device's real name tag, as if the device were there.

sections.title: Subnet, MTU and the Optional 6LBR
sections.content:
The backbone and the federated LLN links are different links in the MLSN, and ND messages are link-scoped, so a 6BBR does not forward them between links. Legacy backbone hosts assume a single link and will not run Path MTU Discovery inside the subnet. So the MTU MUST be the same on the backbone and all federated LLNs, and the 6BBR MUST use the same MTU in RAs on both sides. Link-local traffic, link-scope multicast and hop-limit-1 traffic do not cross between links.

A 6LBR can optionally serve the whole subnet. If one is present, the 6BBR checks with it using an EDAR/EDAC exchange whether a new registration is a duplicate or a move, before running DAD. The 6LBR answers with status 1 (Duplicate Address), 3 (Moved) or 0 (Success). Because other hosts on the backbone may not be registered, the 6BBR still runs classical DAD afterwards.

Registering Nodes MUST implement RFC 8505 and register all of their addresses, or unregistered ones may become unreachable. A prefix is advertised as on-link over the backbone only for compatibility with existing hosts, and MUST NOT be advertised as on-link toward the LLN in Routing Proxy mode.
sections.eli5: All the playground areas must use the same size of ball, and an optional head teacher can keep one master list to settle arguments about names.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC assumes the LLN links are protected against rogue access, and that the backbone is physically secured so that packets cannot be forged or overheard. Classical ND on the backbone has precedence over the proxy, so the threats in RFC 4861 apply in full: any node on the backbone can take over an address with an NA with the Override bit set, forge traffic, or present itself as a router and snoop what it intercepts. Rogue access to the backbone must therefore be prevented at all times, and attached nodes must be fully trusted.

Combining address registration with RFC 8928 gives proof of address ownership via the ROVR field on the LLN, but that protection does not extend over the backbone. An attacker on the backbone can send an NS with an EARO, learn the TID and ROVR from the reply, increase the TID and take over the Binding. Compromised 6BBRs, 6LBRs or 6LRs are also attack points, so all must be trusted.

If classical ND is disabled on the backbone and RFC 8928 plus a 6LBR are mandated, the RFC lists benefits including zero-trust ND flows, less multicast and avoidance of remote ND DoS attacks.
sections.eli5: The helpers can only be trusted if everyone on the playground is trusted. A stranger who gets in can still pretend to be someone else.
